newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-ENQVIST ROLLS PAST SPADEA IN RETURN FROM INJURY.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-ENQVIST ROLLS PAST SPADEA IN RETURN FROM INJURY.

text.p: After a three-month layoff, Sweden's Thomas Enqvist smoothly rolled past American Vincent Spadea 7-6 (7-4) 6-1 Wednesday and into the quarter-finals of the $303,000 Infiniti Open.

"I think I'm playing OK," said the second-seeded, eighth-ranked Swede following the 67-minute sweep which pits him against unseeded Kenneth Carlsen of Denmark on Friday. "I've been away for such a long time. But if I can get some matches I can move up."
Earlier in the day, Carlsen ousted unseeded Armenian Sargis Sargsian 6-4 3-6 6-3.
In night action, third seed Mark Philippoussis overcame another slow start to power past fellow Australian Sandon Stolle 3-6 6-4 6-3.
In the day's lone upset, unseeded Frenchman Guillaume Raoux beat fifth-seeded Patrick Rafter 6-4 7-6 (7-5), dashing any hopes of an Australian quarter-final clash between Davis Cup teammates.
"It's a good win," said Raoux, ranked 80th in the world. "Pat is a good player. Mentally I played a good match. I kept my concentration and played two good points at the end to win."
Rafter said his style plays perfectly into Raoux's strengths.

"He just really enjoys my game," said Rafter, ranked 19th on the ATP Tour. "Everything I do he just seems to be able to counterpunch. I probably didn't play as well as I could have but he was too good for me on the day. He definitely outplayed me off what I had today."

Enqvist is playing his first tournament following a 12-week layoff after tearing a couple of tendons in his left foot while practicing in Monte Carlo on May 19. The injury forced the 23-year-old Swede to miss the summer session, including the French Open and Wimbledon Championships.
But he showed no effects of the injury in posting his first win over Spadea in three tries.
"He's a tough player but today I was the better one," said Enqvist. "I played aggressive and served well. I tried to play my game and I think I played it well today."

Enqvist captured the first set after trailing 4-2. He broke back in the seventh game, and reeled off five of the final six points in the tiebreaker, including a searing cross-court forehand winner at set point.
"When I broke back for 4-3, I thought I played good," he said. "I played more aggressive, and took more command of rallies."
The Swede raced to a 4-0 lead in the second set with a pair of early breaks before closing out the match.
Phillippoussis struggled early for the second time in as many matches before gaining the quarters despite being outgunned nine to seven in aces.
"It doesn't matter to me as long as I get the 'W,'" he said.

After dropping the opening set on a break in the sixth game, Philippoussis trailed 0-2 in the second set. But he levelled the match with a key break as Stolle committed three of his four double faults, including the final two in the 10th game.
Spurred by the gift, Philippoussis, ranked 13th, took advantage and began to turn up the volume on his bullet-like deliveries to as high 136 mph (219 kph).

Philippoussis posted the lone break in the second game of the deciding set when at break point he ran down Stolle's angled backhand volley and cracked a searing up-the line forehand before falling to the ground in excitement.
"When I hit the running forehand I knew it was mine," he said. "I just didn't want to do anything stupid."
